body:
FOUND BY HAND, 2026-08-04, the first time a human drove the login form in a real browser. Myk hit it
immediately; every rail passes. Reproduced and isolated with Chrome DevTools against a live store.

THE MECHANISM, measured end to end:

1. `session.ts:629` and `:645` set `referrer-policy: no-referrer` on the login pages. `oauth.ts:334`,
   `:621`, `:790` set it on the consent pages.
2. With that policy, Chrome serializes the Origin of a form POST as the string `null`. Observed on the
   wire: `origin: null`, `sec-fetch-site: same-origin`, the form-token cookie and field both correct.
3. `fromThisPage` (`session.ts:441-451`) treats a present, non-empty Origin as DECISIVE and refuses
   `Origin: null` OUTRIGHT rather than falling through to the `Sec-Fetch-Site` hint.
4. So a legitimate same-origin form POST is refused: `{"errors":["this request did not come from this
   store's own page..."]}`.

CAUSATION PROVED, not inferred. A proxy that strips ONLY `Referrer-Policy` and changes nothing else
makes Chrome send a real `origin: http://localhost:5821`; login then SUCCEEDS ("Signed in. You are
alice, and you hold the operator role here") and the admin page renders. One variable, opposite
outcomes.

BLAST RADIUS — every session-gated POST in the product:
  - `POST /login` (`session.ts:696`) and `POST /logout` (`session.ts:940`).
  - The consent approval POST (`oauth.ts:712`, calling the same `gate.fromThisPage`) — so the whole
    OAuth authorize flow is unusable in Chrome, which is the flow claude.ai would drive.
  - Every §40 admin POST, which gates through the same helper.
This is not localhost-specific and not transport-specific. It fails behind a TLS terminator too. It has
never been exercised by a human in a browser until today, which is why it shipped green.

WHY THE RAILS MISSED IT, and this is the part worth keeping: `test/server/login-csrf.test.ts:142-143`
tests `{ origin: "null" }` and `{ origin: "null", "sec-fetch-site": "same-origin" }` and asserts BOTH
are refused. The rail encodes the code's premise — "no legitimate flow reaches these doors with a null
origin" (`session.ts:436-439`) — and that premise is FALSIFIED BY THE STORE'S OWN HEADER. A wrong
premise produced a perfect rail around a real bug, which is the exact failure CLAUDE.md's P5 doctrine
names. No rail anywhere drives a real browser, so nothing could have caught it.

THE FIX — two candidates, and the ticket recommends the first:

(a) CHANGE THE POLICY ON PAGES THAT POST: `referrer-policy: same-origin` instead of `no-referrer`.
    Cross-origin privacy is preserved (no referrer leaves the origin) and a same-origin POST keeps a
    real Origin, so `fromThisPage` keeps its strongest form and NOTHING about the check relaxes. This
    is the smaller and safer change. Five call sites.

(b) TREAT `Origin: null` AS ABSENT and fall through to `Sec-Fetch-Site`. The code argues against this
    (a sandboxed same-origin iframe would send `null` + `same-origin`), and that argument is not
    baseless — so this option WIDENS a refusal and needs Myk's judgement. Note the pages already set
    `frame-ancestors 'none'`, and an attacker's own sandboxed frame POSTing here would report
    `sec-fetch-site: cross-site`. Still: (a) achieves the goal without touching the check at all.

RAILS, and the rail is the point:
  - The existing `origin: "null"` cases at `login-csrf.test.ts:142-143` must be RE-EXAMINED, not
    deleted. Under fix (a) they stay valid — a null origin still refuses — and a NEW rail asserts the
    login page does not send `no-referrer`, so the browser never produces null in the first place.
  - ADD A REAL-BROWSER SMOKE RAIL. This class is invisible to a hand-built fixture: every existing rail
    sets Origin explicitly and therefore cannot reproduce what a browser does. One CDP-driven test that
    loads /login, fills the form, submits, and asserts a session opens would have caught this on the day
    phase 6 landed. Cover login, consent, and one admin POST.
  - Two-sided: a genuinely cross-site POST still refuses, and the same-origin browser POST now succeeds.

WHO MERGES: MYK. Fix (a) is small, but this is the authentication and authorization surface, and option
(b) would widen a refusal outright. State in the PR, in one line, which option was taken and what can
now reach the door that could not before.

SEVERITY: the §36/§37/§40 browser surface is entirely unusable in Chrome today. This outranks queue
work.
title: The login door, the consent page and every admin POST are unusable in Chrome — no-referrer makes the browser send Origin: null, and the same-origin check refuses it outright
